title: Legal Research Bench: Measuring End-to-End Reliability in Long-Horizon Legal Research Agents

    Title:Legal Research Bench: Measuring End-to-End Reliability in Long-Horizon Legal Research Agents
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Legal research is a core and time-consuming legal workflow. Lawyers must identify controlling authority, verify that it remains valid, reconcile statutes and cases, and synthesize a grounded answer. Language model agents are a natural fit for this retrieval-intensive workflow, and automating even part of it would be valuable. But that value depends on reliability: a single missing authority, stale citation, or wrong legal conclusion can make an otherwise plausible answer unusable. We introduce \textbf{Legal Research Bench} (LRB), a benchmark of 413 open-ended U.S. legal research questions written by experts, each paired with a gold answer, supporting authorities, and a binary grading rubric. We evaluate thirteen frontier models in a harness with web search, case-law search, page parsing, and retrieval tools. We score agent responses through all-pass grading with source verification, where a response is correct only if every required criterion is satisfied and its cited authorities verify. We also validate the LLM judge against expert attorneys ensuring that benchmark scores track attorney judgment. Agents remain far from reliable: among the models we tested, the strongest, Claude Opus 4.8, is fully correct on 42.9\% of questions. Performance also varies substantially by task setting: all-pass rates differ across areas of law and are lower on questions requiring reconciliation of conflicting authorities. Across models, more turns, tool calls, and inference cost do not predict higher accuracy.

report.summary: New Legal Research Bench finds top legal AI agents fully correct on only 42.9% of expert U.S. legal questions, showing reliability gaps in long-horizon research.
report.background: Legal research is a core and time-consuming workflow: lawyers must identify controlling authority, verify that it remains valid, reconcile statutes and cases, and synthesize a grounded answer. Language model agents are a natural fit for this retrieval-intensive work, and automating even part of it would be valuable. But that value depends on reliability: a single missing authority, stale citation, or wrong legal conclusion can make an otherwise plausible answer unusable. Existing evaluations often do not measure end-to-end reliability with source verification over long horizons. Legal Research Bench introduces 413 open-ended U.S. legal research questions written by experts, each paired with a gold answer, supporting authorities, and a binary grading rubric. It evaluates thirteen frontier models in a harness with web search, case-law search, page parsing, and retrieval tools. Responses are scored all-pass with source verification, and the LLM judge is validated against expert attorneys. The results show agents remain far from reliable, with the strongest model, Claude Opus 4.8, fully correct on 42.9% of questions.
key_points: Legal Research Bench consists of 413 expert-written open-ended U.S. legal research questions, each with a gold answer, supporting authorities, and a binary grading rubric. Responses are scored through all-pass grading with source verification: an answer is correct only if every required criterion is satisfied and its cited authorities verify. The LLM judge was validated against expert attorneys so scores track attorney judgment.

Across thirteen frontier models tested in a harness with web search, case-law search, page parsing, and retrieval tools, the best performer, Claude Opus 4.8, was fully correct on just 42.9% of questions. This means even the strongest long-horizon legal agents fail most expert-level research tasks, often through missing authority, stale citation, or incorrect synthesis.

Performance varies substantially by task setting. All-pass rates differ across areas of law and are lower on questions requiring reconciliation of conflicting authorities. This suggests legal AI reliability is task-dependent and should be reported by legal domain and reasoning demand rather than as a single average.

More turns, tool calls, and inference cost do not predict higher accuracy across models. Simply giving agents more retrieval budget or longer trajectories does not guarantee correctness. Effective authority verification, conflict reconciliation, and answer synthesis matter more than the scale of search activity.

The benchmark validates an LLM judge against expert attorneys, making automated grading more credible for legal research. It also uses source verification, so fabricated, stale, or unsupported citations count against the agent even if the final prose looks plausible. This creates a stricter standard for evaluating legal AI.
report.impact: The benchmark signals that legal AI’s bottleneck is reliability, not fluency. For the AI industry, it raises the bar: vendors must show all-pass, source-verified performance rather than showcase plausible answers. Evaluation will likely move toward expert-designed, end-to-end legal tasks with citation validation. For developers, LRB shows more retrieval turns, tools, or inference spend do not guarantee accuracy; effort should go to authority verification, conflict reconciliation, and uncertainty reporting. For regular users and lawyers, the takeaway is cautious adoption: agents can accelerate finding and drafting, but a single missing or stale authority can make an answer unusable, so human review remains essential. It also gives researchers a measurable target for improving long-horizon legal agents.
report.tools: Watch the Legal Research Bench paper and any dataset or harness released with it. Complementary open resources include CourtListener and the Free Law Project APIs, the Caselaw Access Project, and RECAP for case-law retrieval. Agent evaluation frameworks such as Inspect AI or HELM can help replicate all-pass scoring, while retrieval stacks like LlamaIndex or LangChain can build tool-using legal agents. For citation checking, explore CourtListener’s citation lookup and open legal NLP datasets.
